  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Univariate goodness-of-fit tests with the multiplier bootstrap}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}

---

The function `gof.test()` compares an empirical cumulative distribution
function (CDF) with a fitted CDF. In this example, we test whether independent,
positive observations follow a lognormal distribution with unknown log-scale
mean and standard deviation.

The default is the multiplier bootstrap (`simulation = "mult"`). The main
example uses this default, followed by a parametric bootstrap comparison.

## Run the multiplier bootstrap with numerical derivatives

```{r}
library(fgof)

set.seed(123)
x <- rlnorm(100, meanlog = 1, sdlog = 0.5)
start <- list(meanlog = mean(log(x)), sdlog = sd(log(x)))

set.seed(456)
fit_mult <- gof.test(x, "lnorm", nsim = 199, start = start)
fit_mult$estimate
rbind(statistic = fit_mult$statistic, p.value = fit_mult$p.value)
```

The names in `start` match the arguments of `dlnorm()`. The values initialize
maximum likelihood estimation. For models with a fixed distribution argument,
supply it in `distr.args`. For example, to test a lognormal model with known
`sdlog = 0.5`, supply `distr.args = list(sdlog = 0.5)` and include only
`meanlog` in `start`.

The multiplier bootstrap uses derivatives of the CDF and log-density with
respect to the fitted parameters to account for parameter estimation.
When the derivative callbacks are omitted, as above, `gof.test()` estimates
both derivatives by numerical differentiation. The `ks` and `ksa`
statistics measure the largest absolute difference, while `cvm` and `cvma`
use squared differences. The statistics are evaluated on a quantile
grid (`ks` and `cvm`) or the observations themselves (`ksa` and `cvma`).
Use `gridStat = FALSE` to compute only the observation-based statistics.

## Supply analytical derivatives with automatic differentiation

For a positive observation $x$, write $z = (\log x - \mu)/\sigma$, where
$\mu$ and $\sigma$ are `meanlog` and `sdlog`. The CDF is $\Phi(z)$, where
$\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. The log-density is
$-z^2/2 - \log(\sigma) - \log(x) - \log(2\pi)/2$.

R's `stats::deriv()` generates code that evaluates each expression and
its analytical gradient by applying derivative rules to the expression.
The callbacks extract the gradient matrix, with one row per evaluation
point and columns in parameter order.
[Documentation for `stats::deriv()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/deriv.html)

```{r}
parameters <- c("meanlog", "sdlog")
cdf_with_gradient <- stats::deriv(
  ~ pnorm((log(x) - meanlog) / sdlog),
  parameters, function.arg = c("x", parameters)
)
log_density_with_gradient <- stats::deriv(
  ~ -((log(x) - meanlog) / sdlog)^2 / 2 - log(sdlog) - log(x) -
    log(2 * pi) / 2,
  parameters, function.arg = c("x", parameters)
)

cdf_gradient <- function(theta, x) {
  attr(cdf_with_gradient(as.numeric(x), theta[1], theta[2]), "gradient")
}

score <- function(theta, x) {
  attr(log_density_with_gradient(as.numeric(x), theta[1], theta[2]), "gradient")
}

set.seed(456)
fit_analytic <- gof.test(
  x, "lnorm", nsim = 199, start = start,
  derCdfWrtPar = cdf_gradient, derLogPdfWrtPar = score
)

rbind(numerical = fit_mult$p.value, analytical = fit_analytic$p.value)
max(abs(fit_mult$stat.sim - fit_analytic$stat.sim))
```

Resetting the seed uses the same multiplier draws in both fits. Comparing
the simulated statistics directly shows how closely the two derivative
methods agree, even when the discrete bootstrap p-values coincide.

## Compare with automatic differentiation in RTMB

With RTMB installed, `RTMB::MakeTape()` records the operations that compute
the CDF or log-density at fixed evaluation points. Its `jacobian()` method
then differentiates those outputs with respect to the fitted parameters.
Use `RTMB::pnorm()` inside the tape so that RTMB can differentiate the
standard normal CDF. [RTMB on CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RTMB)

```{r, eval=requireNamespace("RTMB", quietly = TRUE)}
theta <- unname(fit_analytic$estimate)
points <- x[1:5]
log_points <- log(points)

cdf_tape <- RTMB::MakeTape(function(par) {
  RTMB::pnorm((log_points - par[1]) / par[2])
}, theta)

log_density_tape <- RTMB::MakeTape(function(par) {
  z <- (log_points - par[1]) / par[2]
  -z^2 / 2 - log(par[2]) - log_points - log(2 * pi) / 2
}, theta)

c(cdf = max(abs(cdf_tape$jacobian(theta) - cdf_gradient(theta, points))),
  score = max(abs(log_density_tape$jacobian(theta) - score(theta, points))))
```

The two numbers are the largest absolute differences from the corresponding
`stats::deriv()` gradients. Each tape holds the evaluation points fixed, so
build a new tape if those points change.

## Run the parametric bootstrap

```{r}
set.seed(789)
fit_pb <- gof.test(x, "lnorm", nsim = 199, start = start,
                   simulation = "pb")
fit_pb$p.value
```

The parametric bootstrap simulates samples from the fitted lognormal model and
refits the model to each sample. For either bootstrap method, a small p-value
indicates that the observed discrepancy is large relative to those simulated
under the fitted model. A large p-value indicates insufficient evidence against
the model. Choose the test statistic before inspecting the p-values. Increase
`nsim` when the Monte Carlo variability matters for the decision.

See `help("gof.test", package = "fgof")` for the available statistics,
quantile grids, and optimizer controls.
